opus-5.5.text:
I think it's honestly a tough moment for new graduates, and I don't want to sugarcoat it. A lot of the work that used to be the training ground for junior people, like writing boilerplate code, fixing small bugs, running standard experiments, or putting together a first-pass analysis, is exactly what agents are getting good at. From a company's point of view, if one senior engineer with a few agents can do what used to take a small team, the incentive to hire many juniors goes down. So in the short term I do think the entry-level market gets squeezed.

But I'd frame it a bit differently. The question isn't really "junior versus senior." It's whether you're someone who executes well-defined tasks, or someone who can define the task in the first place. Agents are very good when the goal is clear and the feedback is fast. They're still weak at figuring out what problem is worth solving, noticing when the setup itself is wrong, and taking responsibility for the outcome. Those are the skills that matter now, and they don't strictly require ten years of experience. Some new graduates have them, and some senior people don't.

So my advice to students is a few things. First, use these tools heavily, every day, so you understand where they break. If you know the failure modes of an agent better than your manager does, you're immediately valuable. Second, go deep on something. Shallow, broad knowledge is now cheap because the model already has it. Real depth, where you can tell whether an answer is actually correct, becomes the scarce thing. Third, build things end to end and own them. A project you designed, shipped, and debugged yourself, even a small one, says much more than a list of courses.

There's also a structural issue the industry has to face. If companies stop hiring juniors, where do the seniors come from in five or ten years? Somebody has to learn the judgment, and judgment comes from doing real work and making mistakes. I think the companies that figure out a new kind of apprenticeship, where young people work alongside agents and are trained to be the ones directing them, will have a big long-term advantage.

So overall: harder at the entry point, yes. But for people who are curious, who learn fast, and who treat AI as leverage rather than competition, I think the ceiling is actually higher than before. A single person can now do what a whole team used to do, and that applies to new graduates too.

r001.rationale: The response says some graduates can stand out by building and owning projects, and that the ceiling may be higher for curious, fast learners. It does not state that graduates with exceptional, industry-recognized work still have employment prospects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is: it's harder than it was, but not in the way people assume.

The junior tasks that agents do well right now are the ones that are well-specified. You tell it "write a function that does X," "fix this bug," "add a test for this." Those used to be how a new grad spent their first year. So the entry ramp that companies used to provide, where you learned by doing a lot of small, bounded tasks, that ramp is getting compressed. That's real.

But I'd push back on the idea that this means new grads have no path. What's actually happening is the bar is shifting from "can you execute" to "can you judge." Agents produce a lot of output, and someone has to decide whether that output is right, whether the approach makes sense, whether this is even the right problem. In my own work, the bottleneck is almost never typing the code anymore. It's knowing what to ask for and recognizing when the answer is wrong.

So my advice to students is a bit different from what it was five years ago. First, go deep on fundamentals, because that's what lets you evaluate what the model gives you. If you don't understand why an algorithm works, you can't tell when the agent's version is subtly broken. Second, pick a domain and actually understand it, whether that's systems, or biology, or finance, because the value is increasingly in the connection between the tool and the problem. And third, get comfortable working with these tools early. The students who treat agents as a collaborator and still take ownership of the result are the ones I see getting hired.

There's also a timing issue I'd be honest about. Companies are still figuring out how to structure teams around this. Some have overcorrected and stopped hiring juniors, and I think a lot of them will regret that in three or four years when they have no mid-level pipeline. So it may be rough for a couple of cohorts. But the long-run demand for people who can think clearly about hard problems is not going away. If anything, it's going up, because the cost of producing mediocre work has dropped to zero, and the premium on good judgment has gone up accordingly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says some students who use agents well are getting hired and that demand for strong judgment will continue, but it does not state that graduates with exceptional, industry-recognized work retain employment prospects.

astra-6.text:
I think it will become harder, especially if we keep defining entry-level jobs as a collection of tasks that someone more senior hands to you. If an agent can do those tasks, companies may hire fewer people just to execute them. That’s a real challenge for new graduates, because those tasks have also been how people learn.

But doing a task and knowing what task is worth doing are different skills. You still need to understand the problem, judge whether an answer is correct, and figure out what to do when the results don’t make sense. So I would encourage students to use agents, but also build the foundations needed to question them. If you can generate code but can’t explain why it works or diagnose why it fails, you’re in a fragile position.

The opportunity is that a new graduate can now attempt a much more complete project. You don’t necessarily need a large team to turn an idea into something people can try. Showing that you identified a useful problem, built a solution, and improved it based on feedback can be a strong signal to an employer.

That doesn’t mean everyone will easily find a job. Companies also need to think about how they develop future senior people if they stop hiring juniors. But for students, I think the direction is to move beyond completing assignments and practice taking responsibility for a whole problem, with AI as part of the process.

r001.rationale: The response says that completing a useful project can be a strong signal to an employer, but it does not state that exceptional, industry-recognized work preserves employment prospects for new graduates despite agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it will become harder for new graduates, especially if a junior role consists mainly of well-defined tasks that an agent can finish. But doing individual tasks and taking responsibility for a problem are different things. Someone still has to understand what matters, decide whether the result is correct, and work with other people to get it into production.

The challenge is that those junior tasks have traditionally been how people learn. If companies automate them without creating another way to train people, where will their future senior engineers come from? So this is also a problem for employers to solve.

For graduates, I would focus on strong fundamentals and learning to use agents critically. Can you explain why a solution works? Can you catch a plausible but wrong answer? Can you take an ambiguous problem and build something useful? A project where you can discuss those decisions is much more informative than just showing a lot of generated code.

I wouldn’t say there will be no opportunities. The expectations are changing, and the transition could be quite difficult. Being able to learn quickly and exercise judgment will matter a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says opportunities will remain, but does not state that graduates with exceptional, industry-recognized work still have employment prospects.
